Aigues-Mortes is a Rhone River cruise port and town in France's Gard department (Occitanie region) with population around 9,000. The town is best-known for its perfectly preserved surrounding medieval city walls. Aigues-Mortes is located approx 90 km (56 ml) northwest of Marseille (on the French Riviera), approx 33 km (21 ml) southwest of Nimes (Gard department's capital city) and approx 20 km (12 ml) east of Montpellier (Herault department's capital).

The town is also part of France's Petite Camargue (natural region south of Arles and between Mediterranean Sea and Rhone River Delta) featuring as scenery wet plains and lakes. It is separated from Mediterranean Sea by Gulf of Lions but is also connected to the sea via Canal du Rhone a Sete that links Retang de Thau lagoons (Sete) with Rhone River (at Beaucaire). The canal enters the town from northwest and two branches intersect it before exiting (as a single waterway) and flowing into Mediterranean Sea. A railway from Nimes also passes through (northeast to southwest, with a train station in Aigues-Mortes) and links to the coastal terminus Le-Grau-du-Roi. This railway is used for both passenger and sea salt transportation.

As cruise port, Aigues-Mortes is included in the regular schedule of the luxury hotel barge Anne Marie. The boat is owned and operated by one of Europe's largest river cruise companies - CroisiEurope. Aigues-Mortes is one of the easiest cruise stops in the Camargue to explore independently. Cruise calls here are normally made by small hotel barges using the canal-side quays or marina beside the medieval town, so there is no long transfer from a seaport. The fortified center, Tour de Constance and canal excursions are all within easy walking distance.

At a Glance

  • Independent sightseeing: Easy independently.
  • Arrival: Dock alongside the canal; this is not a tender port and there is no conventional cruise terminal.
  • Historic center: A few minutes on foot from the canal-side berths.
  • Best for: Medieval architecture, walking, salt marshes and Camargue scenery.
  • Terrain: The town itself is flat, but streets can be cobbled. The ramparts involve numerous steps and uneven surfaces.
  • Transport needed: None for the old town. A bicycle, taxi or pre-arranged tour is useful for attractions farther into the Camargue.

Getting from the Cruise Port

Small cruise barges normally moor on the Canal du Rhône à Sète around the Aigues-Mortes marina and Quai des Croisades. Exact berths can vary, but the port is immediately beside the fortified town. Passengers can normally walk directly from the vessel toward the Tour de Constance and city walls without a shuttle.

Aigues-Mortes railway station is also close to the walls. Regional trains connect the town with Le Grau-du-Roi and Nîmes, while regional buses serve Nîmes and Montpellier. Public transport is unnecessary for local sightseeing and should only be used for a side trip after checking the return timetable carefully.

Best Ways to Spend Your Time

Explore the Walled Medieval Town

Allow: 1.5–2.5 hours. Independent: Very easy.

Walk through the gates into the compact historic center, with Place Saint-Louis, Notre-Dame-des-Sablons church, small chapels, narrow streets and the almost complete medieval fortifications. Most sights are close together, making this the safest choice for a short call.

Walk the Ramparts and Tour de Constance

Allow: about 1.5–2 hours for the monument itself. Independent: Easy, but moderately strenuous.

The complete rampart circuit is about 1.6 km (1.0 mi) and gives elevated views over the rooftops, canals, salt ponds and surrounding Camargue. The route includes roughly 100 steps, irregular surfaces and exposed sections with little shade. Access to the Tour de Constance and part of the ramparts is adapted for reduced mobility, but the complete circuit is not step-free.

Visit the Aigues-Mortes Salt Works

Allow: about 2–2.5 hours including travel and the visit. Independent: Practical with some planning.

The Salin d'Aigues-Mortes visitor area is roughly 2 km (1.2 mi) from the walled center. Its salt ponds, birdlife and large salt mounds provide the most distinctive landscape around the town. A tourist train operates inside the salt works on scheduled departures and takes about 1 hour 15 minutes.

Walking to the entrance is possible but can be hot and exposed; a bicycle or taxi is more comfortable. Departures are seasonal and can change because of weather or operating conditions, so booking ahead is sensible when the visit is important to your plans.

Take a Camargue Canal Cruise

Allow: 1.5–3 hours depending on the cruise selected. Independent: Very easy.

Local sightseeing boats leave from the Bassin d'évolution near Avenue Tour de Constance, less than 0.5 km (0.3 mi) from the marina. Short cruises follow the Canal du Rhône à Sète through Camargue landscapes, offering an easy nature-focused alternative to additional walking. Check the departure time before committing, as schedules vary by season.

Le Grau-du-Roi and the Beach

Allow: at least 3–4 hours. Independent: Possible with planning.

Le Grau-du-Roi is about 6 km (3.7 mi) from Aigues-Mortes and has a fishing harbor and Mediterranean beaches. Regional trains take about 9 minutes when the timetable fits, but services are not frequent enough to rely on without checking the return first.

A dedicated cycle route also connects the two towns for about 6 km (3.7 mi) each way, largely alongside the canal and wetlands. This is a good option for an active visitor with a long call, but the medieval town and salt works are better priorities on a shorter stop.

Self-Guided Walking Tour

Medieval Aigues-Mortes Circuit

Distance: up to about 4 km (2.5 mi), depending on detours. Pure walking time: about 50–60 minutes. Recommended total: 1.5–2 hours. Difficulty: Easy to moderate; mostly flat with cobbles and uneven paving.

  1. Canal-side berth / Quai des Croisades: Start beside the marina and walk toward the prominent round Tour de Constance.
  2. Tour de Constance: See the town's principal medieval tower. Enter here if you plan to visit the ramparts; otherwise continue at street level.
  3. Porte de la Gardette: Pass the historic main gateway into the fortified town.
  4. Chapelle des Pénitents Blancs: Continue through the quieter northeastern streets to this small historic chapel.
  5. Eastern and southern gates: Follow the inside of the walls toward Porte de la Reine and Porte de la Marine for views toward the salt-marsh landscape.
  6. Place Saint-Louis: Turn back into the center for the main square, statue of Saint Louis and the tourist office.
  7. Notre-Dame-des-Sablons: Visit the town's principal church, just off the square.
  8. Return to the ship: Continue through the western streets toward the Tour de Constance and canal-side marina.

Passengers wanting a more demanding version can add the paid 1.6 km (1.0 mi) rampart circuit. With the tower, walls and town-center stops, allow roughly 3–4 hours rather than trying to rush the complete visit.

When an Organized Excursion Makes Sense

The historic town does not require a guide or cruise excursion. An organized excursion becomes more useful for a wider Camargue visit involving wetlands, traditional horse or cattle farms, wildlife areas or several rural stops. These places are dispersed and public transport is poorly suited to linking them efficiently during a port call.

Nîmes is also possible on a particularly long call, but the regional train journey is about 48 minutes each way and departures are limited. For most cruise passengers, staying around Aigues-Mortes and the Camargue provides a better use of shore time.

Practical Tips

  • The ramparts are very exposed to the sun; carry water and use sun protection in warm weather.
  • Wear suitable shoes for cobbles, stairs and uneven stone surfaces.
  • The color of the salt ponds and the number of flamingos or other birds vary with season and conditions.
  • Check same-day departure times before taking a train, canal cruise or salt-works tour.
  • For Le Grau-du-Roi or any rural Camargue excursion, leave a larger return margin than for sightseeing within the walls.
  • For a short call, the medieval center and ramparts alone provide a complete visit without needing any transport.
